html:
The big picture

The exam is a 90-minute written test with open questions, 80 points in total, 40 to pass, and roughly one point per minute of effort — so a 2-point question wants two short, precise sentences, not a page. The 15–20 questions come from all lecture slides. The sample questions show the mix: definitions (what is a robot?), choosing and justifying a design (robot type, sensor), explaining a principle (time of flight, risk priority numbers), short calculations (unit conversion, efficiency of a chain) and one longer derivation (forward kinematics of a planar arm). The model answers below are suggestions built from the lecture notes, not official solutions.

Exam

  • 90 minutes.
  • Written, pen and paper.
  • Open questions.
  • 80 points in total / 40 needed to pass.
  • 1 point ≈ 1 minute of effort.
  • 15–20 questions across all lecture slides.
  • Keep your answers short and to the point.
Intuition — using the point value

The points tell you how much to write. A 2-point question usually wants two things (a definition + an example, or a choice + one justification). A 4–5-point question wants a principle and its application, or a choice and the numbers that justify it. The 10-point question wants a full derivation with the result. Writing more than the points ask for costs time you'll need elsewhere.

Sample questions

No.QuestionPoints
1What is a robot?2
2A robot is required to transport heavy materials on the factory floor between fixed pickup and delivery points in an automated fashion. What type of robot is suitable for this task? Justify your answer.2
3How does the ToF principle work? Name two different sensors that use ToF.5
4A force sensor is required in a robot design. The robot is expected to experience a force between 5 and 15 N. The sensor's output will be digitised by a voltage measurement system with an input range of 0 to 10 V. Two sensors (S1 and S2) are available; their input–output characteristics are shown below. Which of the two is the most suitable for the application?4
5Derive the forward kinematics for a 3-link planar robot arm (see figure). Link lengths: L_1 = 2\,\mathrm{m}, L_2 = 2\,\mathrm{m}, L_3 = 1\,\mathrm{m}. The joint angles \theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3 are the variable inputs. Compute the end-effector position and orientation for \theta_1 = 45^\circ, \theta_2 = 10^\circ, \theta_3 = 20^\circ.10

Further sample questions:

  • Explain the concept of risk priority numbers and give an example of your choice.
  • The pressure of a hydraulic system is specified as 200 bar. Convert it to \mathrm{N/m^2}.
  • A drivetrain consists of a combustion engine (efficiency 30 %) and a gearbox (efficiency 50 %). What is the total efficiency of the drivetrain?

Question 1 — what is a robot? (2 points)

Worked example — a 2-point answer

A robot is a machine controlled by a computer (program) that performs tasks automatically, replacing human effort; it need not look or act like a human (1 Introduction, Cambridge / Britannica definitions). It typically senses its environment, processes the information and acts on it through actuators.

Two ingredients earn the two points: automatic, program-controlled and does work / acts in the world.

Question 2 — robot for transporting heavy material between fixed points (2 points)

Worked example — choose, then justify

Choice: a wheeled mobile robot, e.g. an automated guided vehicle (AGV) that follows a fixed route between the pickup and delivery stations. Justification: a factory floor is flat, where wheels are the most energy-efficient and stable way to carry heavy loads (legged or aerial robots carry little payload, a stationary arm can't travel); with fixed points the route is known in advance, so simple guidance (lines, markers, a stored map) suffices instead of full autonomous navigation. Three or more wheels give static stability (1 Introduction).

Question 3 — the time-of-flight principle (5 points)

Worked example — principle, formula, two sensors
  1. Principle: the sensor emits a signal (a sound pulse or a light/laser pulse), it reflects off the object, and the sensor measures the time t until the echo returns.
  2. Formula: the signal travels to the object and back, so the distance is d = \frac{v \cdot t}{2}, with v the propagation speed (about 343\,\mathrm{m/s} for sound in air, 3 \times 10^8\,\mathrm{m/s} for light).
  3. Two sensors: an ultrasonic distance sensor (sound) and a LiDAR / laser rangefinder (light). Others: a ToF camera, radar.
  4. Worth a sentence for full marks: light is so fast that LiDAR needs very precise timing (1 ns ≈ 15 cm of distance); sound is slow and its speed depends on air temperature (2 Sensors).

Question 4 — choosing a force sensor (4 points)

S1: about 0–1 V from 0–5 N, then a steep linear part up to about 8.6 V at 18 N, flattening to 10 V at 25 N. S2: linear from 0 V at 0 N to 5 V at 25 N.

Worked example — compare the sensors inside the required range (5–15 N)
  1. S1 in 5–15 N: this is its steep, linear section: slope \approx \frac{8.6 - 1}{18 - 5} \approx 0.58\,\mathrm{V/N}; output from 1 V to about 6.8 V. Linear over the whole range and within 0–10 V.
  2. S2 in 5–15 N: slope \frac{5}{25} = 0.2\,\mathrm{V/N}; output only 1 V to 3 V — 20 % of the 10 V input range.
  3. Decide: S1. Its sensitivity is about three times higher, so the converter's fixed voltage resolution corresponds to a three-times finer force resolution, and it is still linear and inside the input range. S2 would work but wastes most of the measuring range.
  4. The trap: S1 is nonlinear overall (kinks at 5 N and 18 N) — but outside the required range only, so that doesn't count against it.
Why does using more of the input range give a better measurement?

The A/D converter splits its range into a fixed number of steps — e.g. 10 V over 1024 steps is about 10 mV per step (9 Measurement and Signal Processing). A sensor that spreads the 5–15 N range over 5.8 V uses about 590 of those steps; one that squeezes it into 2 V uses only about 200. More steps per newton means a smaller quantisation error in newtons and a larger signal compared to the noise.

Question 5 — forward kinematics of the 3-link planar arm (10 points)

Planar arm: \theta_1 measured from the horizontal, \theta_2 and \theta_3 each relative to the previous link; link lengths L_1, L_2, L_3.

Unclear (slide 5)

The angles are printed as "\theta_1 = 45^\circ, \theta_2 = 10^\circ, \theta_1 = 20^\circ". The second \theta_1 must be \theta_3 = 20^\circ — the three joint angles are the inputs.

Worked example — derivation and numbers
  1. Absolute link angles (each joint angle is relative to the previous link): link 1 at \theta_1, link 2 at \theta_1 + \theta_2, link 3 at \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3.
  2. Add the link vectors:
\begin{aligned} x_e &= L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2) + L_3\cos(\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \\ y_e &= L_1\sin\theta_1 + L_2\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2) + L_3\sin(\theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3) \\ \phi_e &= \theta_1 + \theta_2 + \theta_3 \end{aligned}

(Symbols: x_e, y_e — position of the end effector (m); \phi_e — its orientation, measured from the horizontal; L_1, L_2, L_3 — link lengths (m); \theta_1, \theta_2, \theta_3 — joint angles, each relative to the previous link.) (Equivalently, chain homogeneous transforms: R(\theta_1)\,T(L_1,0)\,R(\theta_2)\,T(L_2,0)\,R(\theta_3)\,T(L_3,0) — 5 Coordinate Transformation and Kinematics.)

  1. Angles: 45^\circ, 45^\circ + 10^\circ = 55^\circ, 55^\circ + 20^\circ = 75^\circ.

  2. Position:

    • x_e = 2\cos 45^\circ + 2\cos 55^\circ + 1\cos 75^\circ \approx 1.414 + 1.147 + 0.259 = 2.82\,\mathrm{m};
    • y_e = 2\sin 45^\circ + 2\sin 55^\circ + 1\sin 75^\circ \approx 1.414 + 1.638 + 0.966 = 4.02\,\mathrm{m}.
  3. Orientation: \phi_e = 75^\circ from the x axis.
  4. Plausibility check: the reach is \sqrt{2.82^2 + 4.02^2} \approx 4.9\,\mathrm{m}, just under the fully stretched L_1 + L_2 + L_3 = 5\,\mathrm{m} — the arm is nearly straight, as the small angles \theta_2, \theta_3 suggest.
Common mistake

Using each joint angle on its own: x = L_1\cos\theta_1 + L_2\cos\theta_2 + L_3\cos\theta_3. That treats \theta_2 and \theta_3 as angles from the horizontal, but they are measured relative to the previous link — the angles must be accumulated. Here it would give x \approx 4.32\,\mathrm{m}, y \approx 2.10\,\mathrm{m}, a completely different point.

Risk priority numbers

Worked example — explain + example

Concept: in an FMEA, each possible failure mode is rated (typically 1–10) for severity S, occurrence O and detection D (10 = practically undetectable). Their product, \mathrm{RPN} = S \cdot O \cdot D, ranks the risks so countermeasures go to the highest numbers first (8 Introduction to Human-Robot Interaction). Example: a cobot's proximity sensor drifts slowly: S = 6, O = 5, D = 7 → \mathrm{RPN} = 210. Its emergency-stop button fails: S = 9, O = 2, D = 3 → \mathrm{RPN} = 54. The drift is treated first, e.g. with a daily self-test that lowers D.

Pressure conversion

Worked example — 200 bar in \mathrm{N/m^2}
  1. Conversion factor: 1\,\mathrm{bar} = 10^5\,\mathrm{Pa} = 10^5\,\mathrm{N/m^2}.
  2. Multiply: 200 \cdot 10^5 = 2 \times 10^7\,\mathrm{N/m^2} (= 20\,\mathrm{MPa}).
  3. Sense check: hydraulics run at 100–300 bar (3 Actuators), so tens of MPa is right.

Efficiency of a drivetrain

Worked example — efficiencies in series multiply
  1. The engine passes on 30 % of the fuel's power: \eta_1 = 0.3.
  2. The gearbox passes on 50 % of what it receives: \eta_2 = 0.5.
  3. Total: \eta = \eta_1 \cdot \eta_2 = 0.3 \cdot 0.5 = 0.15 = 15\,\%.
Common mistake

Adding or averaging the efficiencies (80 % or 40 %). Each stage only passes on its fraction of what it received, so the fractions multiply — a chain is always less efficient than its worst link.
